paper_metadata.title: Prolonged epileptiform EEG runs are associated with persistent seizures in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study uses a well-defined cohort of JME patients with long-term follow-up. While the sample size is small (n=40), the inclusion/exclusion criteria and baseline characteristics are clearly described, and the recruitment source is a stable regional population.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: The study was based on 42 previously reported patients with JME, originally identified for a study on the association to human leukocyte antigens in 1992 (Moen et al., 1995).
items.reasoning: The source is a previously established cohort with known clinical characteristics.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: Most patients resided in the primary catchment area of the hospital, Sør-Trøndelag county, with only one neurological and EEG department; thus facilitating this form of long-term follow-up.
items.reasoning: The use of a single regional center for a specific catchment area reduces referral bias.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: originally identified for a study on the association to human leukocyte antigens in 1992... In 2012, 40 of these patients were available for seizure outcome assessments
items.reasoning: The timeline from initial identification to follow-up assessment is clearly stated.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Department of Neurology and Clinical Neurophysiology, St. Olav's Hospital, Trondheim, Norway
items.reasoning: The specific clinical setting and geographic location are provided.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: The clinical diagnosis of JME was based on the ILAE-classification from 1989 (Commission, 1989).
items.reasoning: Standardized international diagnostic criteria were used for inclusion.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: In 2012, 40 of these patients were available for seizure outcome assessments 31 years (range 20–68 years) after epilepsy onset
items.reasoning: 40 out of 42 original patients (95%) were followed up, which is an excellent participation rate for a 20+ year study.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Demographic and clinical data, as well as treatment characteristics are shown in Table 1.
items.reasoning: Table 1 provides comprehensive baseline data including age, sex, age at onset, and seizure types.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study achieved a very high follow-up rate (95%) over a multi-decade period. The reasons for the loss of the 2 patients are not explicitly detailed, but the impact on the overall analysis is negligible.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: 40 of these patients were available for seizure outcome assessments
items.reasoning: 95% of the original cohort was analyzed.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The prognostic factors (EEG features) were measured using standardized protocols (SCORE) and, crucially, the assessors were blinded to the clinical outcomes, which significantly reduces measurement bias.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: Prolonged epileptiform runs were defined as generalized epileptiform activity lasting ≥3 s
items.reasoning: The primary prognostic factor (run duration) is explicitly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: EEG recordings were retrospectively reviewed with blinding for clinical outcome.
items.reasoning: Blinding of the EEG reviewers to the outcome is a strong methodological safeguard.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: lasting ≥3 s, as this duration is supposed to significantly impact cognitive function (Aldenkamp et al., 2005).
items.reasoning: The 3-second cut-off was based on prior literature regarding cognitive impact, not post-hoc data dredging.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: The international 10–20 system for electrode placement was used.
items.reasoning: Standardized EEG methodology was applied across the cohort.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: EEG-data on paper or in digital form was available for rescoring in 40 patients.
items.reasoning: All 40 patients had available EEG data for analysis.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: Imputation was not mentioned; however, the study used 'relative occurrence' to handle varying numbers of EEGs per patient.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The outcome (seizure freedom) is clearly defined, but it relies on clinical assessment/patient report over a very long period, which may be subject to recall bias. However, the 5-year remission threshold is a robust clinical marker.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: 21 were in the seizure free (SF) group (in remission for more than 5 years) and 19 were in the persistent seizure (PS) group.
items.reasoning: The outcome is clearly dichotomized with a specific time threshold (5 years).

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: Information on seizure control after at least 20 years of clinical follow-up was available for 40 patients
items.reasoning: While clinical follow-up is standard, it relies on patient/caregiver reporting which is less objective than the PF measurement (EEG).

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: 40 of these patients were available for seizure outcome assessments 31 years... after epilepsy onset
items.reasoning: All patients underwent the same clinical outcome assessment protocol.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study acknowledges and analyzes major confounders like AED use and diurnal variation. However, the retrospective nature and the 'pseudo drug resistance' (lifestyle factors) could not be fully controlled, and multivariable adjustment was not performed due to the small sample size.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: We have considered various potential confounders, such as the influence of AED treatment effects and the diurnal variation
items.reasoning: Key clinical confounders were identified and recorded.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: AEDs at final follow-up... AEDs ever used
items.reasoning: Medication types are listed, but specific doses/durations for every EEG point are not fully detailed.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Treatment (AEDs at recording) and diurnal characteristics associated with recordings
items.reasoning: Confounders were linked directly to the time of the EEG recording.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Table 8 Treatment (AEDs at recording) and diurnal characteristics
items.reasoning: The same data collection framework for confounders was applied to all.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Exact time of the day was known for 108 recordings
items.reasoning: Missing data (e.g., time of day) was simply treated as 'Unknown' rather than imputed.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: The distribution of patients across AEDs were similar in patients with and without prolonged runs
items.reasoning: The authors checked for balance between groups but did not use design-stage control like matching.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: EEG features in the two prognostic patient groups... were compared using Fisher exact test... Mann–Whitney test
items.reasoning: Only univariable analyses were performed; no multivariable adjustment (e.g., Logistic Regression) was used to control for confounding.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical methods are appropriate for the small sample size. The authors are transparent about the limitations of multiple testing and the retrospective nature of the data.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: Data analysis was performed using SPSS version 21... compared using Fisher exact test for categorical 2 × 2 data, while the non-parametric Mann–Whitney test was used
items.reasoning: The statistical plan is clearly laid out.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: Main EEG variables were selected based on previous reports regarding the prognostic significance of EEG in JME
items.reasoning: Variable selection was hypothesis-driven based on existing literature.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: non-parametric Mann–Whitney test was used to compare numerical data (e.g. relative occurrence variables) between groups.
items.reasoning: Non-parametric tests are appropriate for the small sample size and likely non-normal distribution of EEG counts.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: We found no statistically significant association between the prognostic groups and the occurrence of normal EEG findings... (data not tabulated).
items.reasoning: The authors report both significant and non-significant findings across various EEG parameters.
